Posted January 23, 2001
The Medical Marijuana Problems Analysis by Richard Cowan

My good friend Alan Bock of the Orange County Register has written a new book on medical marijuana, Waiting to Inhale,

Bock is a great writer and this is the first history of the medical marijuana movement. I hope to review the book soon, but its arrival today made me want to review some of philosophical and political problems presented by medical marijuana for both the prohibitionists and the anti-prohibitionists.
See
The Orange County Register Editorial Page Does the Best Job of Explaining the Significance of the Supreme Court’s Ruling on the Oakland Case.
and
Alan Bock Gives An Excellent Overview Of The Prospects For Medical Marijuana

In 1993, when I was National Director of NORML, Allen St. Pierre -- now the National Director of the NORML Foundation -- and I felt compelled to get NORML more involved in the medical marijuana issue.

Although NORML had filed the first lawsuit -- back in 1972 -- to force the Federal government to reschedule marijuana, the organization has always focused primarily on the non-medical use issues.

However, we really felt compelled to become more involved in the medical issue. After all, we could hardly say that we don’t care about the suffering of the sick and dying, which certainly exceeds that of most of the healthy victims of marijuana prohibition.

Nonetheless, that was a very dark time indeed, and a number of activists were concerned that NORML was going to abandon the marijuana prohibition issues and concentrate just on medical marijuana. That was not at all the case, but it was another objection to the medical marijuana issue -- before it took on a life of its own.

Thus, medical marijuana presents different people with different philosophical and political problems that both its proponents and opponents generally ignore.

Libertarian psychiatrist Thomas S. Szasz has – as usual – his own thought provoking problem with medical marijuana, and that is a useful place to start.

Szasz’ objection is very simple. He argues that there should not be a loophole for medical use, because the government has no business telling anyone – sick or healthy – that they do not have a right to use it -- for whatever reason.

In an interview in the July 2000 issue of Reason Magazine, Szasz said, " I find the general rule unacceptable, and the exception is simply doing one particular favor to one particular person or group of persons. "
See http://www.reason.com/0007/fe.js.curing.html

I think that he is right, but we still cannot turn our backs on the patients. In times of war and other emergencies, children, the elderly, the sick and dying, et al., are given special treatment. In this war we have to do everything possible to protect the most vulnerable victims, but that does not mean that victimizing others can be justified.

Taking a different approach, my friend Dennis Peron upset many of his colleagues in the marijuana reform movement when he said that " all (adult) use is medical. "

Szasz would argue that this is irrelevant. The government simply has no business deciding whose use is medical or not. Again, I think that he is right, but that does not take care of the immediate needs of the patients. Dennis did.

Frankly, the Federal and various state and local governments have behaved so badly that – in addition to Szasz’s general philosophical objections -- there is the basic point that officialdom is not acting in good faith and cannot be trusted.

Two prominent examples of this are the former Drug Czar Barry McCaffrey’s lying about his own Institute of Medicine report and former California Attorney General Dan Lungren’s claiming before the election that Prop 215 would legalize marijuana for everyone – then saying that it allowed only 2 plants after the election.
See
The First Anniversary of the IOM Report And The Lies and Hatred Continue, Business As Usual. Analysis By Richard Cowan
and
The First Anniversary of the IOM Report And The Lies and Hatred Continue, Business As Usual. Analysis By Richard Cowan

This sort of behavior gives rise to a sort of pragmatic libertarian argument. Whatever the case for any government program, it just will not work in the hands of the appalling people who govern us. Never mind the more philosophical arguments.

Ironically, this particular line of argument also works against the current approach to medical marijuana favored by most activists and the public in general -- that doctors should be allowed to decide whether a patient can get medical marijuana.

In the context of our present medical system that makes a certain sense. After all, we trust doctors to control access to most other " medicines " – with the exception of those deemed safe enough to be sold over-the-counter.

There are two problems with this.

The first is simply that marijuana is safer than most – perhaps all – of the over-the-counter medicines.
See
Lethal Dose Of Cynicism From Makers Of Tylenol Poll On Aspirin Dangers
– Context Of Medical Marijuana Debate

However, the bigger problem is that organized medicine has behaved so badly regarding medical marijuana that there is no reason to trust them either, regardless of the philosophical objections raised by Szasz.
See
Column By Authors of the IOM Report On Medical Marijuana
Shows Why The Public Does Not Trust The Medical Establishment –
And Why They Should Not! With Analysis by Richard Cowan

Interestingly, the public seems to agree in a very odd way. The initiatives generally require patients to have a doctor’s recommendation for a medical marijuana exemption, even though almost every marijuana initiative approved by the voters won in the face of opposition by the state medical association. Thus the voters rightly trust most doctors individually, but rightly distrust the organized quackery of the medical establishment.
See
Maine Passes Medical Marijuana Initiative By 61%
Against Almost Unanimous Establishment Opposition

Prohibitionists like to argue that initiatives are not a good way to approve a medicine, but the initiatives don’t actually do that. They really just exempt certain people – sometimes not even everyone who needs medical marijuana – from marijuana prohibition. That is what Szasz finds so objectionable. Indeed, why should anyone have to ask anyone for permission to use a plant? In the current regulatory context, the government in DEAland has very limited control over other plant medicines, herbs -- except when it can invoke the Drug War.

The overarching ambition of the government to gain control of everything we ingest can be seen in the FDA’s repeated attempt to get control over herbs and vitamins. The health food industry has beaten them every time. Now the DEA is about to find itself in a war with this very powerful group, when it moves to ban hemp seed oil products for human use.
See
Hawaiian Representative Says DEA Plans to Ban Hemp Products Before Bush Takes Office.

Hemp seed oil is a very important supplement for many people. It is one thing to ban medical marijuana, which is identical to non-medical marijuana. It is quite something else to ban a food product because they claim that a few people have beaten a positive " drug test " by claiming that it was caused by THC in hemp seed oil. When the health food industry counterattacks – as they will – they may find themselves wondering about the government’s suppression of the single most important and versatile herbal medicine. If they do not think about this, we will remind them.

The FDA model is itself the source of another objection to " medical marijuana " by its foremost academic advocate. Lester Grinspoon in Marihuana, the Forbidden Medicine, argues that marijuana’s medical potential will never be realized until it is fully legal because the current medical paradigm just cannot deal with a plant having multiple ingredients, as opposed to single molecule pharmaceutical products. Again, never mind the philosophical arguments, " the medical system " just cannot handle the medical use of a complex plant.
See
Dr. Grinspoon Asks, " Why won't government let us use marijuana as medicine? " -- As UK Developer of " Water Soluble " Cannabis Says, " I would make cannabis available on the NHS now. "

The point here is that the medical marijuana movement has to do everything possible to defend the patients, whose interest is essentially immediate, while recognizing that this is only a stop gap. The fact is that the system, meaning organized medicine, the FDA, the DEA and law enforcement at every level has shown itself to be incompetent at best and more often treacherous and malicious.

Being candid about the long-term impossibility of an exclusive medical marijuana system may feed the paranoid fantasy being pushed by the prohibitionist that medical marijuana is just trick to legalize marijuana, but they have been lying about it anyway, so worrying about the prohibitionists is pointless.
See
Fooling Our Children’s Children: Lying About the Medical Marijuana Movement;
Is There Any Difference Between The Drug Czar and A Crackpot?

In fact, the philosophical problems that the anti-prohibitionists have with medical marijuana pale by comparison with those of the prohibitionists.

In some ways, I think that medical marijuana is God’s little trick on the prohibitionists. After all, they had gotten away with outlawing the least dangerous drug, while promoting, even subsidizing the most dangerous drugs.

Then, one by one people with a wide variety of illnesses used marijuana for what some doctors like to call its undesirable side-effect – euphoria – and discovered that it also gave them symptomatic relief from their illness – and sometimes slowed or even arrested its progress.

It is important to understand that until very recently most patients did not use marijuana because they had heard about its medical value. They were " recreational " users, just getting an illegal grin, like any of the millions of others who have been arrested.

In other words, if it were not for the criminality of these early medical marijuana users, there would be far less known about its medical uses. Of course scholars like Grinspoon and others would have written about it, but the fact is that Marihuana, the Forbidden Medicine was blacked out by the mainstream media that made Listening to Prozac a best-seller at the same time.

Medical marijuana initiatives don’t win because people have read books about it, but because at this point most people know people who have used it medically. That is why they ignore the establishment, medical and otherwise.

Now the prohibitionists are trapped. They have lost the medical marijuana argument, but they cannot retreat. They have lashed themselves to the mast of a fast sinking ship. Marijuana prohibition may just sink altogether because the prohibitionist blocked medical use that could never have threatened prohibition – if marijuana were as dangerous as they claimed.

Of course, that is the rub. And the paradox. Because the medical marijuana movement was forced for political reasons to give doctors control over access to the plant – to which Szasz rightly objects, huge numbers of people using marijuana under medical supervision and there is now a vast body of clinical data being developed by medical users.

It is still being ignored by the medical establishment for what it shows, that marijuana really does have many medical uses. But it is not being ignored by the public.

However, like the dog that didn’t bark, the clinical data may actually be more important for what it does not show.

Understand that the FDA system actually depends on clinical observations of the side-effects of pharmaeuticals to detect any problems that the double-blind " scientific " testing system may have missed. FDA approved drugs are recalled because of serious problems reported in the clinical settings. Where are these problems with marijuana? The absence of these " side-effects " actually has more significance for the " recreational " use of marijuana than for its medical use. After all, some of the most useful drugs over-the-counter drugs can have lethal side-effects.

And that is why the prohibitionists are locked into the suppression of medical marijuana at all costs and why any acceptance of medical marijuana by the establishment will hasten the end of marijuana prohibition.

That is the best answer to Dr. Szasz’ philosophical arguments.
